title: Software Testing · Chapter 3
description: Testing throughout the life cycle: SDLC and development models, test levels, test types, and maintenance testing.

topics.title: SDLC & Development Models
topics.description: SDLC phases, waterfall, V-model and iterative-incremental models.

questions.prompt: Which phase sequence matches the SDLC used in this subject (RDDTDS)?

options.text: Design → Requirement → Develop → Deploy → Test → Support
Requirement → Design → Develop → Test → Deploy → Support
Requirement → Develop → Design → Test → Support → Deploy
Develop → Design → Requirement → Test → Deploy → Support

questions.explanation: RDDTDS = Requirement, Design, Develop, Test, Deploy, Support. (PADIT — Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Testing — is the other common version.)

questions.prompt: In the SDLC Design phase, what does HLD stand for?
questions.explanation: HLD = High Level Design; LLD = Low Level Design.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs to LOW level design (LLD) rather than high level design?
questions.explanation: LLD covers program specs, database design, data access design, interface design and class specifications. Functional design, activity flows and program inventory are HLD.

questions.prompt: Which items belong to the REQUIREMENT phase of the SDLC? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Requirements include functional requirements, DFDs, ER diagrams, state transition diagrams, system parameters, external interfaces and acceptance criteria. Class specs are LLD.

questions.prompt: Which are tasks in the DEVELOP phase? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Develop = environment setup, test data creation and coding. User training happens in Deploy.

questions.prompt: Which are tasks in the DEPLOY phase? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Deploy includes data conversion/migration, database creation, production tests, contingency planning, user training, production support and enhancements. Test specifications belong to the Test phase.

questions.prompt: Which statements are MYTHS about the SDLC? (select all that apply)

options.text: Until I get the program running, I have no way of assessing its quality
Once the program is written and working, the job is done
Testing activities should start early in the development cycle
For every development activity there is a corresponding test activity

questions.explanation: The two myths are that the job is done once the program works, and that quality can't be assessed until the program runs (reviews can assess it earlier).

questions.prompt: Which are the three software development models covered in this chapter? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: WVI: Waterfall, V-model and Iterative-incremental. Big-bang is an integration testing strategy, not a development model.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of phases in the waterfall model (RDIVM)?
questions.explanation: RDIVM: Requirements, Design, Implementation, Verification, Maintenance.

questions.prompt: What are the disadvantages of the waterfall model? (select all that apply)

options.text: It uses too many short development cycles
Fixing defects involves a high cost

questions.explanation: Waterfall flows one way: non-iterative, inflexible, and defects found late are expensive to fix.

questions.prompt: Which diagram represents the V-model?

image.alt: Two circular Plan, Build, Test cycles side by side, with an arrow leading from the first cycle to the second.
Boxes going down the left side to Code at the bottom, then back up the right side, with dashed lines linking each left box to the right box opposite it.
Five boxes stepping diagonally downwards, each with an arrow to the next (Requirements, Design, Implement, Verify, Maintain).

questions.explanation: The V-model goes down through the development phases and back up through the test levels, with each development phase mirrored by a test level. A is waterfall; C is iterative-incremental.

questions.prompt: How does the V-model differ from the waterfall model?

options.text: It develops the system as a series of short cycles
It is built on the waterfall concept but adds a mirrored test-planning and validation level for every development phase
It has no testing phase at all
It links all units together at once and tests them

questions.explanation: The V-model keeps the sequential waterfall flow but mirrors each development phase with a matching test level.

questions.prompt: In the V-model, which test level goes in the box marked “?” (between component testing and system testing)?

image.alt: V-shaped diagram. Left side going down: User requirements, System requirements, High-level design, Low-level design, then Code at the bottom. Right side going up: Component testing, a dashed box with a question mark, System testing, Acceptance testing. Dashed lines link each left box to the box opposite it.

questions.explanation: The four V-model levels (CISA) are Component, Integration, System and Acceptance testing. Integration testing is mirrored with high-level design.

questions.prompt: The V-model must always have exactly four test levels.
questions.explanation: The V-model may have more, fewer or different levels depending on the project and product.

questions.prompt: Which describes the iterative-incremental model?

options.text: All modules are tested together only at the end
Every development phase has a mirrored test level
Development flows steadily downwards through each phase once
Requirements, design, build and test are done as a series of shorter development cycles

questions.explanation: Iterative-incremental development repeats requirements → design → build → test in short cycles.

questions.prompt: Which are examples of iterative-incremental development models? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: RRAP: RAD, RUP, Agile and Prototyping. Waterfall is sequential.

questions.prompt: What does RAD stand for?
questions.explanation: RAD = Rapid Application Development, an iterative-incremental model.

questions.prompt: Which are tips for good testing in any development model? (select all that apply)

options.text: For every development activity there is a corresponding test activity
Include testers early in reviewing development documents
Adapt the model to the project rather than using it 'out of the box'
Test analysis and design should begin in parallel with the corresponding development stage
Only start testing once all coding is complete

questions.explanation: Testing should start early and run in parallel with development, and models must be adapted to each project.

topics.title: Test Levels
topics.description: Component, integration, system and acceptance testing; incremental vs big-bang; alpha vs beta.

questions.prompt: Which are test levels listed in the notes (CISAIB)? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: CISAIB = Component, Integration, System, Acceptance, Incremental, Big-bang. Regression testing is a test TYPE (testing related to changes).

questions.prompt: Which test level searches for defects in separately testable software such as modules, programs, objects and classes?
questions.explanation: Component (unit) testing verifies separately testable pieces of software.

questions.prompt: Where are test cases for component testing derived from? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Component test cases come from the component specification, software design or data model.

questions.prompt: Who usually performs component testing?

options.text: The developer who wrote the code

questions.explanation: Component testing is usually done by the developer who wrote the code.

questions.prompt: Component testing may include non-functional characteristics (e.g. memory leaks) and structural testing (e.g. branch coverage).
questions.explanation: Besides functionality, component testing can cover resource behaviour, robustness and structural coverage.

questions.prompt: Which test level tests interfaces between components and interactions with other parts of the system, such as the OS, file system or hardware?
questions.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interfaces and interactions.

questions.prompt: What are the two types of integration testing? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: There are two types: component integration testing and system integration testing.

questions.prompt: Who normally performs integration testing?

options.text: The developer who wrote the code

questions.explanation: Integration testing is normally done by independent testers.

questions.prompt: Only functional approaches can be used for integration testing.
questions.explanation: Both functional and structural approaches may be used.

questions.prompt: Modules M1, M2, M3… are first unit-tested individually, then combined ONE BY ONE and tested for successful interaction. This is…
questions.explanation: Incremental testing combines modules one at a time and tests each interaction.

questions.prompt: An integration strategy in which all units are linked at once, resulting in a complete system, is called…
questions.explanation: In big-bang testing all units are linked together at once.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of big-bang testing?

options.text: It can only be done by customers
It takes too many test cycles
It requires every module to be tested individually first
It is difficult to isolate errors, because the interfaces across individual units were not verified

questions.explanation: With everything linked at once, it is hard to tell which interface caused a failure.

questions.prompt: System testing is concerned with…

options.text: Whether the customer accepts the system
Only the interface between two modules
The behaviour of the whole system / product

questions.explanation: System testing looks at the whole system or product.

questions.prompt: Which statements about system testing are true? (select all that apply)

options.text: It is done by the customer at their own site
It is done in a controlled environment
It investigates both functional and non-functional requirements
Its goal is to see if the software meets its requirements
It is done by an independent testing team

questions.explanation: System testing is done by an independent team in a controlled environment, checking functional and non-functional requirements.

questions.prompt: Whose responsibility is acceptance testing?

options.text: The developer who wrote the code

questions.explanation: Acceptance testing is the responsibility of the customer or user.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of acceptance testing?

options.text: To find as many defects as possible
To establish confidence in the system
To test the interfaces between modules

questions.explanation: Acceptance testing aims to establish confidence. Finding defects is not its main focus.

questions.prompt: Acceptance testing is always the final test level.
questions.explanation: Acceptance testing is not necessarily the final level in testing.

questions.prompt: Testing performed at the developer's site by testers who are internal employees of the organisation is…
questions.explanation: Alpha testing happens at the developer's site with internal testers.

questions.prompt: Testing that commonly uses black-box techniques, performed by clients outside the organisation at the end-user's location, is…
questions.explanation: Beta testing is done by real users outside the organisation, in their own environment.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe ALPHA testing? (select all that apply)

options.text: Reliability, security and robustness are checked
It requires a testing environment or lab
It involves both white-box and black-box testing
Developers can immediately address critical issues

questions.explanation: Reliability, security and robustness are checked in BETA testing, not alpha.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe BETA testing? (select all that apply)

options.text: It does not require a testing environment or lab
It is performed at the developer's site
Most feedback is implemented in future versions of the product
Reliability, security and robustness are checked
Only one or two test cycles are run

questions.explanation: Beta testing runs at the end-user's site, so it doesn't need a lab; it's the alpha testing that happens at the developer's site.

questions.prompt: In which type of acceptance testing are reliability and security NOT checked? (alpha or beta)
questions.explanation: Reliability and security are not checked in alpha testing; they are checked in beta testing.

topics.title: Test Types
topics.description: Functional, non-functional, structural, and confirmation & regression testing.

questions.prompt: Which are the four test types? (select all that apply)

options.text: Testing related to changes (confirmation and regression)

questions.explanation: The four test types are functional, non-functional, structural, and change-related (confirmation & regression). Big-bang is an integration strategy.

questions.prompt: All test types can be applied at every test level (component, integration, system and acceptance).
questions.explanation: Yes — all test types can be implemented at all CISA levels.

questions.prompt: Functional testing is concerned with…

options.text: The internal structure of the code

questions.explanation: Functionality describes WHAT the system should perform.

questions.prompt: Non-functional testing is concerned with…

options.text: HOW GOOD (how well) the system works

questions.explanation: Non-functional testing checks software and system attributes: how good the system works.

questions.prompt: What is the test basis for functional testing? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Functional tests are derived from requirements, use cases and functional specifications. Control flow is the basis for structural testing.

questions.prompt: Functionality can also be undocumented, for example the legitimate expectations of the customer.
questions.explanation: Not all functionality is written down; legitimate customer expectations count too.

questions.prompt: Which of these are NON-FUNCTIONAL tests? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Non-functional tests include performance, suitability, load, maintainability, stress, reliability and portability testing.

questions.prompt: Structure-based testing is based on…

options.text: The internal structure of a component or the architecture of the system

questions.explanation: Structure-based testing uses the internal structure or architecture.

questions.prompt: What can structure-based testing be based on? (select all that apply)

options.text: The structure of abstract models such as a finite state machine
The calling hierarchy of procedures or structured menus

questions.explanation: Structural testing uses control flow, calling hierarchies/menus and abstract models such as finite state machines.

questions.prompt: What is the objective of structure-based testing?

options.text: To cover all elements of the considered structure

questions.explanation: Structural testing aims to cover all elements of the structure being considered.

questions.prompt: Where is structure-based testing mainly applied?

options.text: Component and integration testing (and as an addition at higher levels, e.g. menu structures)

questions.explanation: It is mostly used in component and integration testing, and sometimes at higher levels.

questions.prompt: What is regression testing?

options.text: Testing a brand-new program for the first time
Linking all units together at once
Executing previously defined test cases on a modified program

questions.explanation: Regression testing re-runs existing tests on a modified program.

questions.prompt: Why is regression testing done?

options.text: To make sure software changes have not adversely affected previously existing capabilities
To decide whether the customer accepts the system
To check that the test environment is set up
To find the root cause of a defect

questions.explanation: It ensures changes haven't broken what already worked.

questions.prompt: Trying to remove an item from a queue BEFORE it has been placed into the queue is an example of which regression error type?
questions.explanation: Inappropriate control sequencing errors are side effects of changes in execution sequence.

questions.prompt: Bottlenecks and deadlocks are examples of which regression error type?
questions.explanation: Resource contention errors include bottlenecks and deadlocks.

questions.prompt: Side effects caused by SHARED DATA are which regression error type?
questions.explanation: Data corruption errors are side effects due to shared data.

questions.prompt: Timing and storage utilisation errors are called performance ______.
questions.explanation: Performance deficiencies include timing and storage utilisation errors (the P in DIRP).

questions.prompt: Which are techniques of regression testing (RRP)? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: RRP: Retest all, Regression test selection, Prioritisation of test cases.

questions.prompt: Which regression technique re-executes every test in the existing suite, and is very expensive in time and resources?
questions.explanation: Retest all runs the whole suite, so it is the most expensive technique.

questions.prompt: In regression test selection, test cases are categorised into which two groups?
questions.explanation: Reusable test cases can be used in later regression cycles; obsolete ones cannot.

questions.prompt: Prioritisation of test cases selects tests based on…

options.text: Business impact, and critical & frequently used functionality
Which tests were written most recently

questions.explanation: Prioritising by business impact and critical/frequent functionality greatly reduces the regression suite.

topics.title: Maintenance Testing
topics.description: Testing an existing operational system after modification, migration or retirement.

questions.prompt: Where is maintenance testing done?

options.text: Only on individual components during development
Only at the developer's site during alpha testing
On a brand-new system before its first release

questions.explanation: Maintenance testing is done on an existing operational system.

questions.prompt: What triggers maintenance testing? (select all that apply)

options.text: Migration of the software or system
Writing the very first version of the code
Modification of the software or system
Retirement of the software or system

questions.explanation: Maintenance testing is triggered by modifications, migration or retirement.

questions.prompt: Planned enhancement changes fall under which maintenance trigger?
questions.explanation: Modifications include planned enhancement changes.

questions.prompt: Operational tests of BOTH the new environment and the old environment are part of…
questions.explanation: Migration includes operational tests of the new environment as well as the old one.

questions.prompt: Testing of data migration or archiving is required when a system is ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Retirement of a system includes testing the data migration or archiving.

questions.prompt: Maintenance testing is performed before a system is first released into operation.
questions.explanation: Maintenance testing is done on an EXISTING operational system, after release.
